item.title: Software factories and code reviews with Harjot Gill
item.description: CodeRabbit CEO Harjot Gill explains how he shipped over 5,000 pull requests in a month, why he believes human code review is dead, and what he gets from spending $250,000 a month on AI.
item.dc:creator: Gergely Orosz
item.content:encoded:
Listen and watch now on YouTube, Apple, and Spotify. See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom.

Brought to You by

• turbopuffer – a ridiculously scalable, fast and cheap hybrid search engine, built on top of object storage, used by cutting-edge companies like Anthropic, Linear, Ramp and many others. Many companies that switch to turbopuffer are cutting their search bills by 50% or more and getting much faster results. Check it out.

• Entire – Entire launched its own Git forge, shipped Continuous Memory, and reinvented the pull request (called Trails). Trails are a much more natural workflow when agents keep pushing new changes, after iterating on feedback – and you have more context and control on when a change is ready to merge. Check it out

• WorkOS – WorkOS built Airlock, the authorization layer for AI agents. It evaluates every request against the agent’s intent + your rules, and either allows it, denies it, or routes it to a human. Works with Claude Code, Codex & MCP gateways. Learn more

In this episode

In this conversation, we step into the world of an AI-pilled CEO to explore how their startup works. This episode might as well be a way of succeeding that contradicts the growing convention that AI spending costs are too high and must be clamped down on.

Harjot Gill is founder and CEO of CodeRabbit, an AI code review business, and he shipped over 5,000 pull requests last month, spending on AI at a monthly run rate of $250,000(!) It’s certainly not a conventional approach and Harjot gets into detail about the thinking and reasoning behind it.

In this episode of The Pragmatic Engineer Podcast, we talk about his background in building software and founding infra startups for the last 30 years, and how things changed into the era of building software factories at CodeRabbit. We talk about why he believes human code review is dead, and how his team maintains quality while shipping at unprecedented speed.

We also get into the rising costs of AI development, why Harjot is convinced that tech startups need more funding than ever, and how AI is changing recruitment and the skills for success.

Takeaways from the conversation with Harjot

1. Janitorial work formed a large part of his 5,000 PRs last month, pushed with agents. He sets off his agents to improve systems like the CI, fixing flaky tests, and refining caching. A lot of the PRs are generated during his commute, and at evenings and nights. In a few cases, he steers agents to make the UI feel better. Examples of stuff Harjot has built:

  • A write-ahead log (WAL) on top of object stores using Rust (the agent ran for six weeks!). This WAL is now in production.

  • Migrating all of CodeRabbit’s services over to Bun – running over a weekend

  • A new CI system after the previous one had performance issues

2. CodeRabbit spends millions of dollars per month on AI, with a team of 40 engineers. Harjot estimates that a PR costs him around $150 in a personal spend of around $250-$275K per month. He compares it to marketing teams with 10 marketers at VC-funded companies who can drive $100M in spend. I point out that his startup is an outlier; the AI spend I hear about elsewhere is in the region of between $200-$2,000 per month, per dev. Finding out how this spend makes sense was one reason I was keen to meet Harjot.

3. For dev tooling startups like CodeRabbit, massive AI spend can be justified by launching new, AI-related products faster. It feels to me that CodeRabbit is not a typical company: its AI spending is a form of R&D if it creates new solutions that can be commercialized and sold. It’s not the same at places with fixed customer bases willing to pay a certain amount for an existing product, and no more.

Also, Harjot says that they got quoted $13M/year for a CI solution to handle their PR output, but the price made him decide they’d build their own CI system using agents. It took a week, and the new CI cost 50% less than the quote, with similar performance.

4. In 2021, Harjot believed AI would write most of the code. When working at FluxNinja, Harjot found that code review was already becoming a bottleneck, with GitHub Copilot’s autocompletions somewhat speeding up writing code. He misjudged the potential market size, assuming only larger companies that bought code verification solutions like Snyk and SonarSource, would buy AI-code review tools – instead, it’s pretty much everybody!

5. Harjot believes agents need to be “hill climbing”; they need to have ways to verify their own work

These are the layers that he believes are necessary, including ones he and the team use:

  • Formal models like TLA+ and Lean. For one of their products, the engineering team utilized TLA+, and found race conditions that the code review overlooked. More recently, Harjot is experimenting with another formal method, Lean.

  • Local deterministic simulations. One of the infra pieces built at Harjot’s startup is a simulation harness to fuzz different interleavings (concurrent operations).

  • Emulating real APIs. Harjot mocks up and emulates APIs like Google Cloud APIs as part of testing.

  • Dev environments. Agents can spin up services in environments like Google Cloud and Vercel, and confirm they work correctly on development deployments

  • Production: staged rollouts. Harjot believes in releasing features with feature flags, and doing progressive rollouts. He said they often have an agent observe the performance characteristics of the rollout, check the logs, and continue the wider rollout when things are stable. This last part reminds me of OpenAI’s Perf Factory inside its software factory.

6. Human code review is dead, long live the human review! Harjot thinks that we will stop reviewing code generated by agents. Instead, we’ll spend more time reviewing the planning and final asset. Inside of CodeRabbit, engineers are reviewing releases (multiple PRs), not individual PRs.

7. Engineers can be banned from committing without human review. The company has a “review exempt list” of devs who can push to production without anyone reviewing their releases. When an outage happens, the team traces the PR that broke prod, and the dev who pushed it gets a ‘strike.’ Rack up enough strikes and releases have to be reviewed by colleagues. I personally like this idea of giving trust to devs to push to prod, but pairing it with accountability: the trust gets revoked if you cause production to be unstable!

8. Fine-tuning models stopped being worthwhile. CodeRabbit used to invest in fine-tuning models used in AI review, but Harjot says that new frontier models moving faster means that it would be tough to maintain their own fine-tuned ones, so it’s not worth it.

9. There are “war rooms”. To get important stuff done, engineers, product folks, and designers gather in the room and steer the agents as together they build a prototype, then a working product. This approach reminds me of Uber in 2016, except ‘war room’ efforts took 2-3 weeks, people flew in from different offices, and it meant aligning on the plan and putting a rudimentary prototype together. The teams finished the remaining work over a matter of months.

10. What Harjot looks for when hiring engineers: agency, breadth of experience, and systems thinking. He posted an unconventional job ad, only inviting candidates who had shipped 1,000+, non-slop PRs in the past 30 days, or had played 500+ hours of strategy and management games like Civilization, Age of Empires, Transport Tycoon, or Factorio. Harjot says he cannot unsee the similarities between running dozens of agents in parallel and playing a strategy video game involving tracking what dozens of units do.

Additional thoughts

This conversation gave me lots to think about. My kneejerk reaction was to question why anyone would spend so much on AI each month; I would assume it’s just wasteful. So, I’m delighted to learn more about where Harjot is coming from. I sense he is pushing the limit of what a single human developer can do when running hundreds of agents in parallel, and he still has more ideas than can be built. Plus, he doesn’t have to worry about his AI spending budget!

Could spending be much cheaper for the same usage? Harjot and CodeRabbit are paying frontier API costs, not using open models. We cover how profitable coding use cases are for inference vendors and frontier companies due to KV cache nuances in this week’s inference deepdive, and how the $200/month Max plans for individuals and small businesses offer usage closer to $8,000-14,000/month in API usage, due to the same KV cache profitability detail. Moving to open models could surely reduce a good part of this spend, but at the cost of some capability.

The engineer + strategy gamer combination helps push AI agent usage? Harjot is not some nontechnical “vibe coder”: he’s been coding for 30 years, and mostly used Neovim before moving over to AI agents. He’s long been obsessed with infra and distributed systems, and in his younger years, played Civilization. He detects parallels between the two activities and it’s interesting that he incorporated them into a job description.

The “Dracula effect” is real with AI agents. I often see the “Dracula effect” of AI agents draining people, like Steve Yegge mentioned in February. Harjot also reports disturbed sleep, like waking up at night to nudge his agents.

Well-funded AI-pilled startups could enjoy a massive upside of building with AI. Over the course of our conversation, I started to understand why it makes sense for Harjot and CodeRabbit to spend so much on AI. They need to build solutions that AI-native startups want to use, and CodeRabbit being AI-pilled itself confers the advantages of firsthand insights and empathy with customers. There’s much that can be learned from how Harjot and CodeRabbit work, all while this approach looks set to remain niche at a time when most companies are tightening the reins on AI spend.

CodeRabbit’s business is being an AI infra startup, and the time-to-market with new products is a massive differentiator. In that context, it makes sense for CodeRabbit to build a lot of software internally and then productionize some of it, contributing to their revenue and valuation possibly increasing down the road. I find it useful to learn about such approaches, even if you decide that this direction would not be feasible for yourself, your team, or company.

item.title: Inference engineering for software engineers
item.description: When is the right time to drop APIs provided by the frontier AI labs, and what about choosing models & providers, caching, dedicated GPUs, KV cache concerns, and more? A practical deepdive
item.dc:creator: Gergely Orosz
item.content:encoded:
A recent trend we’ve covered is of tech companies moving to open models to rein in AI spend: Uber cut its per-token costs by 50%, Pinterest by 90%, and even AT&T has achieved a 56% decrease. But how do you move from a frontier lab’s APIs to using open models? There are two options:

  • “Bare metal:” With plenty of time and money, you can go “bare metal” and purchase a few dozen NVIDIA GPUs and use those AI supercomputers, like Revolut has done: running 56 separate B200 units itself to serve its inference needs. This is a lot of work to set it up, but after that, operational costs are as cheap as it gets.

  • Inference provider: most companies contract with an inference provider that operates large fleets of GPUs, and makes it easy for customers to onboard and start using open models fast.

Onboarding to an inference provider to run LLM workloads comes with challenges, such as dealing with tail latencies, worrying about cache hit rates, rate limits, and more. Inference engineering is a set of engineering practices that we believe is increasingly beneficial for software engineers to familiarize themselves with. To go deeper into this area, we’ve talked with three leading inference providers to learn more: Modal, Fireworks AI, and Baseten. Today, we cover:

  1. What are inference providers & how do they differ from AI labs? They have GPU infrastructure similar to frontier labs, don’t train their own frontier models and are experts at hosting open models.

  2. When to switch from frontier labs? The most common reasons are to reduce costs, have more control over latency, and to fine-tune AI models.

  3. Choosing a model, provider, and deployment strategy. Use evals to find the right open model for your use case, evaluate vendors, and decide between multi-tenant API usage and dedicated GPUs.

  4. Stage #1: API replacement using a multi-tenant inference setup. The easiest way to onboard to an inference provider is to “swap” the API of a frontier lab to an API of an inference provider. But there may be latency problems and caching issues at high loads.

  5. Signs you’ve outgrown multi-tenant inference APIs. Hitting rate limits, performance consistency problems, and overpaying for usage are signs that it might be time to adopt dedicated GPUs.

  6. Stage #2: Configuring dedicated GPU nodes. With dedicated GPUs, you’ll need to get into the details: size of the model, interactivity versus throughput, KV cache sizing, failover options, and more.

  7. Speculative decoding. If there’s unused compute during the decode phase, you might consider a Speculator to further boost inference performance.

As usual, we have no affiliation with vendors mentioned in this article, and have not been paid to mention any company. Special thanks to Richard Gong (Inference lead, Modal), Dmytro Dzhulgakov (cofounder and CTO, Fireworks), and Philip Kiely (Special Projects at Baseten) for sharing details about inference engineering challenges.

1. What are inference providers & how do they differ from AI labs?

Inference providers are companies that sell access to LLMs which they run on users’ behalf. From the outside, this isn’t so different to what OpenAI and Anthropic offer: an API endpoint, ability to stream tokens, and pay based on token usage.

But what makes inference providers different from frontier labs is the models running behind the endpoint: inference providers run open-weight models, whereas frontier labs train their own models. In this field, Modal, Fireworks, and Baseten each operate slightly different strategies:

  • Modal sees itself as a cloud infrastructure provider that focuses on making its offering programmable via its SDKs. It natively supports inference services through its SDKs, but leans heavily on the open source ecosystem for running its inference workloads efficiently. Performance tweaks to its stack are merged upstream. In the words of Richard Gong, Inference Lead at Modal: “when you run code on Modal, you should be able to see all the code that’s running.”

  • Fireworks positions itself as a provider for specialized AI workloads. Most of its business is in dedicated deployments, which often include fine-tuning and provision of latency guarantees. Much fine-tuning and post-training is available for self-service. Fireworks also offers forward-deployed researchers that can help with post-training custom models or components. Dmytro Dzhulgakov, Fireworks’ CTO, says: “our tagline is specialized intelligence, which means we will tune everything from model to infrastructure for your particular use case.”

  • Baseten describes itself as an all-in-one place to build agents. It starts with the basic infrastructure layer with uptime guarantees, flexible commercial terms, without vendor lock-in. Baseten builds additional layers for building agentic workloads on top of its inference platform. These additional layers include sandboxes, governance services, and self-serving, post-training functionality.

To customers, inference providers offer LLM APIs that can be used as drop-in replacements for frontier labs’ APIs. However, inference providers are not the same, as suggested above:

  1. Inference providers don’t pre-train their own foundational models. A single pre-training run for frontier-level LLMs can cost millions of dollars, and only hyperscalers and specialized frontier labs can afford it. Inference providers run post-training on open-weight models because it’s significantly cheaper.

  2. Competitive pricing. The main business of inference providers is offering open-weight models at competitive rates.

  3. Dedicated hardware. A big part of the appeal of inference providers is the ability to have dedicated hardware for users to interact with vendors on the infrastructure layer.

  4. Efficiency & customization. Inference providers offer similar commoditized open models, and compete heavily on efficiency and customization services.

As an example of efficiency, Fireworks announced its Ember-1 model in September 2026, that is post-trained on the Kimi K3 foundation, delivering a similar quality level but with 40% fewer reasoning tokens consumed. Consuming far fewer reasoning tokens gives Fireworks an edge on cost compared to a vanilla Kimi K3 model.

In general, frontier labs have poor uptime, and this helps inference vendors win market share. API Uptime provided by frontier labs isn’t at the levels expected of modern cloud providers: currently, the self-declared uptime of Anthropic is 99.5%, and for OpenAI it’s 99.97% for API, and 99.2% for ChatGPT. These numbers are well below the four nines (99.99%+) uptime expected of cloud providers – which is something that a vendor like AWS is known to uphold.

Imagine you’re a developer aiming to provide a 99.99% uptime guarantee for your application; you can’t rely on a single frontier LLM provider for the service’s critical path. But in the graphs above, degraded performance slots aren’t counted as downtime. As all these APIs are multi-tenant, it means that performance degradations will naturally hit some tenants – with no way to be aware of the degradation, or do anything about it.

Reliability is an ongoing concern with the LLMs of frontier providers and inference providers. Even though many inference vendors offer higher reliability guarantees than frontier models, inference providers can also go down, too. For companies that use inference providers, it’s common to use an LLM gateway with fallback logic to another provider – or to a frontier API. We explored this in a deepdive with Ramp, whose LLM router project started with this exact problem statement.

2. When to switch from frontier labs?

Moving from frontier AI labs to an independent inference provider is often driven by three factors: cost, control, and the need for more customization.

Most common reason: cost

Many companies start considering inference providers because they have pressing cost concerns. In many cases, a frontier model is more capable than necessary for most requests, meaning a “dumber” model is just as good for simpler tasks – and nobody would notice the difference! In such cases, it’s a “no-brainer” for an engineering team to choose to route some requests to a cheaper model hosted by an inference provider.

“Smart routing” is an obvious way to cut costs. An LLM router – the “smart router” – is prompt-aware and can route an LLM request to the most cost-efficient provider that can solve the request. This is an approach that fuelled Uber’s ~50% cut in per-token costs this summer.

Providers offer OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible API endpoints, so switching providers is trivial. All that is needed is to point your app at the new endpoint operated by a “smart router.”

But how to decide which model to serve? Generic benchmarks are often insufficient because they usually do not fully represent a team’s traffic patterns. Most inference providers ask for prompt samples or eval sets in order to gauge which model best serves a customer’s use case. The experience of using a new LLM endpoint resembles using APIs provided by frontier labs, while API calls are still charged per token, and response time SLAs generally don’t exist.

More control over latency

When you use a frontier lab’s endpoint, there is little control over operational issues like response latency and model availability. Opting for a dedicated setup with an inference provider offers full control over both:

  • Latency: model response times are more predictable because the app has dedicated capacity that can scale by usage.

  • Model availability: Engineers can run the model of their choosing on their dedicated GPUs and keep operating it as long as needed, avoiding the risk of a frontier lab changing models from one day to the next.

Fine-tuning model quality: customization

When an inference stack runs on dedicated hardware with open source models, it’s possible to work with inference providers to finetune a model’s quality as required, which optimizes latency or throughput performance. Richard Gong of Modal says that around 10% of their customers go this far, suggesting that customization is for “power users”.

Fine-tuning a model’s quality is typical in two scenarios:

  • Tweaking a smaller model: achieving a similar level of quality with a smaller model, with fewer parameters. This performance gain is achieved via performance tweaks not possible with off-the-shelf models. Inference providers allow you to post-train a smaller model for your specific use case. A post-trained small model can then outperform the original model in those specialized scenarios.

  • Fine tuning for niche use cases. Improving quality when general purpose models aren’t good enough, often because the data isn’t publicly available. For example, projects in the legal and medical sectors tend to benefit from this, according to the Fireworks team.

3. Choosing a model, provider, and deployment strategy

Most inference providers offer the exact same models to run, and the differences lie in model performance and quality. For example, model quality can differ by default context length, and some providers cap this to below what the model supports. There’s also quantization to consider, where a model’s weights are compressed to a lower numerical precision, or default temperature aka controlling how random the output is. Here’s a practical approach for selecting a provider:

  1. Model: Choose an AI model to switch to

  2. Provider: pick an inference provider to host the model, based on model quality, performance, and cost

  3. Deployment model: decide whether to use a multi-tenant service, or to move to dedicated GPU nodes

Choosing a model

The most obvious way to decide which model to use is to run an eval set against the various model options. In the latest episode of The Pragmatic Engineer Podcast, Microsoft’s CEO Satya Nadella argues that private evals shall be a big component of tech companies’ intellectual property (IP) in the future. He says:

“Public benchmarks are great, but your private evals will matter more: you need your own eval for the outcome that matters to you. Then you look at performance across all these models and continuously optimize.

Our customers start with a frontier model, then say: ‘I’ve got all those traces. This is a deterministic workflow, so I don’t need the next big model drop. I want to optimize the cost.’ They drop in [another] model, use the traces to fine-tune it – and there you have it.”

An example of public benchmarks is from Artificial Analysis that maintains an eval set to compare costs for generic tasks across different models. Here are the average costs per task, broken down by model:

Let’s say you build an app on top of Anthropic’s Sonnet 5.5 model, costing $5.46 on average per task in the index. If Kimi K3 is sufficient for this use case, then that model is ~60% cheaper to run at only $2.00 per task. Note that the cost comparison here is per-task, not per-token. This makes sense because different models require different numbers of tokens to complete a task, which makes it harder to compare model costs without your own private evals!

Having said that, deciding whether a model is good enough requires more than just looking at public benchmark results. Ideally, there’s an eval set to compare models with. In the absence of that, running an A/B experiment is a good alternative. For example, if you want to switch agentic coding workflows to an inference provider, you could simply let some engineers use the new model and give feedback on the results.

Choosing a provider

All providers tweak open models to squeeze out more performance without degrading quality too much. Therefore, model outputs and quality vary among providers. A useful tool for comparing providers’ model accuracy is Artificial Analysis’ endpoint accuracy index. This is a score that benchmarks results from various inference providers against its own, self-hosted version. An index value of 100% means the provider’s results are the same as Artificial Analysis’ own hosted model.

Endpoint accuracy is broadly similar and the scores of providers range from 93% to 102%. The variance comes from performance and quality tweaks that inference providers make to their versions of open models. Since LLMs are non-deterministic, this measurement has a 95% confidence interval – which adds another layer of complexity to evaluation. Minor score differences are considered within the same level as Artificial Analysis’ reference model, hence the green coloring of bars that are technically below 100%.

Deployment model: multi-tenant or dedicated?

All providers’ offerings include a multi-tenant API, as well as dedicated GPUs to run LLMs. This deployment progression is typically a graduation path: most deployments start as drop-in API replacements of frontier labs’ APIs, and as usage grows they start switching to dedicated infrastructure.

When switching to an open model hosted by an inference provider, the per-token cost decreases. However, you are still running in a multi-tenant environment, which comes with similar performance bottlenecks, like when using the API endpoint of a frontier model. The difference is that with an inference provider, you can migrate to a dedicated hosting environment and have full control over a deployment’s performance. Having your own deployment (controlling the GPUs with the inference provider) makes it possible to fine-tune a model’s quality with techniques such as post-training.

Typical graduation path from multi-tenant API to dedicated GPUs

The most typical path for a startup using LLMs:

  1. Use a frontier lab’s API endpoints

  2. Move over to using an open model, using the API endpoint of an inference provider

  3. Rent dedicated GPUs from the inference provider

Moving to an inference provider is usually coupled with achieving some kind of product-market fit. All three inference providers we spoke with told us that by the time a customer signs up by getting to “stage 1” (see below), their product has gained traction in the market. Per-token costs only become important with non-trivial levels of user activity.

“Stage 2” with dedicated GPUs is a level that implies significant budget commitments, a more mature product, and large-scale usage.

Getting inference capacity: this can be tricky, given the global GPU shortage! We previously covered how there’s a CPU shortage inside cloud providers – and so there should be no surprise that there’s an even more pressing GPU shortage. Even large inference providers are having a hard time getting all the GPUs they need. The inference providers we talked with all run on top of several cloud providers – plus some also manage their own bare metal – exactly to get as much capacity as they can. Getting access to more GPUs justifies the added operational complexity from running in multiple clouds. Being able to quickly onboard new cloud providers that have spare capacity is becoming a key differentiator in the industry.

If you need dedicated GPUs, know that it will probably be expensive. Scarce capacity is one of the reasons why getting a dedicated setup typically requires long-term budget commitments upfront. To put it simply: you’ll need to pay a larger amount, and commit for paying for those GPUs on a longer timeframe.

4. Stage #1: API replacement, using a multi-tenant inference setup

For teams with hefty LLM bills, the easiest way to decrease cost is to replace frontier labs’ models in Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, with a frontier-level open model. Looking at data from OpenCode and OpenRouter, the current most popular choices of engineering teams for this include DeepSeek 4.1 Flash, GLM 5.3, and others including Kimi K3.1 Pro.

The easiest way to carry out a replacement is to point an application to an API provided by the inference provider. In practice, this means using a multi-tenant API where other customers will be hitting the same endpoint, similar to using an API endpoint from a frontier lab. At first, everything will be great, but then you may come across problems of time-to-first-token (TTFT) latency, caching-related costs, and latency issues.

These are also problems of using APIs from frontier labs, the difference being that with inference providers, there’s the option of solving most of them by moving over to a dedicated deployment.

Latency problems: TTFT, inference time, user-experienced latency

Time-to-first-token is a measure of how long it takes from the moment a request hits the LLM API, to when the client starts receiving the first tokens. The distribution of TTFT latencies has a long tail:

A long right tail means that a significant proportion of requests have double the median latency or longer. So, when measuring latencies, the p95/p99 latencies are just as important as p50 latencies. TTFT can be measured in two places:

  • Inference time: provider-instrumented TTFT shows the pure inference time. Some providers expose this metric to customers on dashboards, while some include it in their responses. Frontier labs typically do neither.

  • User-experienced latency: client-instrumented TTFT shows the full user-experienced latency, including things like network transport, or the TLS handshake.

Server-side inference is just one part of the overall time that an app’s user spends awaiting a response. To achieve truly fast p95 times for user latency, it’s best to consider optimizations like connection pooling on the LLM API consumer side.

When serving LLM APIs on shared infrastructure, inference providers run many copies of the LLM inference engine that serves customer requests. A single inference engine can serve multiple requests concurrently. A new replica is created when the number of concurrent requests exceeds the current replica capacity. Scaling of replicas is one reason why inference-only TTFT latencies vary so much.

Other reasons why TTFT can vary:

  1. ‘Noisy neighbour’ effects: a request is batched with another request that’s more expensive to process, so it takes longer than if the request was in a batch with a similar request.

  2. Cold start: happens when a request is waiting in a queue because there is no capacity in existing replicas. The inference provider is creating new replicas but this isn’t instantaneous, so a request has to wait until the new replica becomes available (until the new replica starts up, from a “cold”, offline state).

  3. Cold cache: when sending a large request for the first time, it may end up on a replica without the relevant KV cache loaded (the cache is “cold” – which is the opposite of “hot cache” when the KV cache is already populated). An inference provider will typically try to keep requests sticky to the same replica because that keeps replica’s KV cache hot. Sometimes, this isn’t possible because your cache expired, or it landed on the replica that doesn’t have the relevant KV cache. KV cache then has to either be copied from cold storage if available, or if it’s not, fully processed before the first token can be generated.

Prompt cache utilization is observable and actionable by engineers building on LLM APIs. You can get prompt cache utilization metrics from the response of the OpenAI completions API. Building your apps to effectively exploit prompt cache is a key technique in improving app performance, so it’s worth taking a closer look.

Caching issues: cost and latency

Most major LLM API endpoints today are stateless REST APIs, inspired by OpenAI’s chat completions API.

LLM endpoints are stateless, which creates problems because most LLM use cases are stateful. Dmytro Dzhulgakov, cofounder and CTO at Fireworks calls the decision to make the API stateless “the original sin” because while the client app behaves like it’s talking to a stateless API, the burden is on the provider to ensure efficient caching mechanisms in a distributed environment.

item.description: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella on AI’s impact on software engineering, code verification, and engineers’ careers.
item.dc:creator: Gergely Orosz
item.content:encoded:
Listen and watch now on YouTube, Apple, and Spotify. See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom.

Brought to You by

Many companies that switch to turbopuffer are cutting their search bills by 50% or more and getting much faster results. Check it out. Also, check out the new and improved The Pragmatic Engineer search I built on top of turbopuffer!

In this episode

What does software engineering look like when generating the code becomes cheap and verifying it is the hard part?

There can be few people in tech more qualified to tackle this hot topic than Satya Nadella. Microsoft’s CEO started his career as a software engineer – a rare thing among Big Tech CEOs. Satya joins me to discuss how building software is changing at Microsoft, and what it means for us, software engineers.

We start with Microsoft’s embrace of open source from the mid-2010s and the lessons learned from building VS Code in the open. I ask how Microsoft went from holding an early lead with GitHub Copilot to having to catch up with Cursor and Claude Code, and what it reveals about building products around rapidly improving models.

Satya also explains what a “software factory” means to him, why specifications and verification are becoming more important, and how teams that work on products like the Windows operating system are adapting. We also touch on Microsoft’s voluntary exit offers, AI-related anxiety around engineering careers, and hear Nadella caution against drawing long-term conclusions from the slowdown in junior hiring.

We also explore open and local models, why companies need to control their own AI infrastructure, and how to build safeguards around increasingly capable agents. Satya also has some advice for engineers who want to excel during this period of change – and why he would like to spend more time on building.

Sidenote: we recorded this episode in Redmond just a few hours before Microsoft’s day-long Outlook outage, so there was no discussion of it. To the people asking: no, I did not pull out any cables during my visit that might have kicked out that outage :) However, I am already talking with the team inside Microsoft on-point for this outage, and expect a more detailed follow-up in the newsletter on what went wrong and what we can learn from it.

Takeaways from the conversation with Satya

I appreciated how grounded and thoughtful Satya was – and how pragmatic he is in suggesting to verify anything and everything related with LLMs, and not blindly trust anything or anyone (including vendors or AI models!) 12 of the most interesting takeaways I noted:

1. A new form of software engineering: teams building software factories to improve their work. Satya cites the Azure networking team which manages 500+ fiber network operators and recently built an agentic system to better manage emails and processes. Now, they operate much more efficiently as a result. Satya sees this as the reality of “AI transformation”: brownfield work on building software factories to improve how teams operate, all while continuing the day-to-day work.

2. GitHub Copilot fell behind Claude Code because the IDE faded out in just six months. Dev tools are in Microsoft’s DNA, but it was completely unprepared for Claude Code retiring the concept of the IDE in favor of the command line. Satya admits this move by Anthropic caught them off guard, and it taught him that when a non-linear model jump occurs, the form factor of using that model can change fast. He also admits the IDE “faded away” over the course of just six months, and Microsoft’s stronghold in dev tools had been the IDE, with VS Code. It sounds like Microsoft learned a lesson here and is now more nimble with dev tools, and less attached to past form factors.

3. “Own the intelligence”: avoid lock-in & treat agents as an insider risk. Satya cautions companies to avoid lock-in with any single model provider by ensuring that the harness, memory, and model are not coupled, so that they can be changed with ease. He also thinks more companies should consider using open models as a way to protect their core intellectual property (IP) from leaking out, and build private evals to decide what models to use and upgrade to. He also says that models are intelligent but unreliable, so it’s best to treat them as “insider risks” and build a separate system to verify that agentic systems work as expected.

4. Microsoft is betting on “hybrid intelligence.” Satya questions why we rely on the cloud for AI infrastructure when last year’s frontier-equivalent model can already run on a laptop, while the frontier-equivalent model from as recently as the previous quarter can run on desktops. He predicts the concept of “hybrid intelligence” will gain traction, of having local AI models running on laptops and desktops, and a model router deciding when to use cheap, “unmetered” local models, and when to route to a more capable, expensive one in the cloud. Microsoft is building infra to support such routing with its Microsoft AI (MAI) models and Surface Laptop Ultra lineups.

5. Code generation has become cheap, but verification is still hard. Satya reveals he’s been thinking a lot lately about how challenging it is to verify the correctness of code generated today. Models doing a “critique” on generated code is one solution, but it involves model alignment issues, such as a model achieving its goal in undesirable ways; for example, making tests pass by deleting failing tests. Satya also thinks we’ll start to build more verification loops based on production traces, in a kind of “recursive self-improvement” (RSI). But for this, models need to be able to verify fixes, meaning we return to the verification problem! We didn’t arrive at any definite solutions for this during the conversation, which tells me this is a problem space that will keep many of us engineers busy!

6. What’s with those voluntary exit offers? I asked Satya directly why Microsoft recently made voluntary exit offers to most of its software engineers for the first time in the company’s history. I also wanted to know if it could mean layoffs in the future. Unsurprisingly, his reply was diplomatic, and my more direct interpretation is this:

  • Large transformations/reorgs are likely because teams will change in size (many getting smaller) and function, with many new AI-related teams being formed.

  • There’s high demand internally for new, AI-related roles like forward-deployed engineers.

  • A voluntary exit offer can motivate engineers who feel “stuck” on their current team (for example, if there’s less opportunity to do AI-related work) to take interviews elsewhere, and, with an offer in hand, depart with a smaller “bonus.” Satya admits that even inside Microsoft, not all teams got the memo about becoming more AI-native. Those affected can accept a voluntary exit offer until December, and it’s safe to assume many are indeed interviewing at other places!

  • There is a lot of change ahead. My take is that any “pre-AI” company will have to restructure itself, not just Microsoft. At least Satya is candid about it.

7. The cause of the junior hiring slowdown is that companies are figuring out the new way to work. I asked if Microsoft is hiring new grads and juniors, and Satya admits there’s a slowdown there (and at many places). He identifies a process that’s currently taking place as the reason why:

  • There’s an internal reorg happening on team sizes and roles

  • Teams are figuring out how to build “software factories” and how to balance human cost/effort and token budgets

  • When all this is figured out, then junior recruitment will pick back up

At Microsoft, most teams are busy coming up with new ways of working, so it’s not a good time to bring in new hires. Satya expects this “reorg” phase to be temporary, after which hiring will pick up.

8. Microsoft has started a “preceptorship” program for AI-accelerated development. In collaboration with Carnegie Mellon University, Microsoft launched the PRAISE program (Preceptorship for AI-accelerated Software Engineering). It’s actually a concept borrowed from nursing, where new nurses are paired with experienced ones to develop real-world experience and confidence. Preceptors are experienced software engineers who coach “preceptees” on using AI tools thoughtfully, while building strong systems thinking, taste, and judgement. This is the kind of program I wish more companies would consider partnering with educational institutions on; perhaps this one will inspire other engineering leaders.

9. The next big engineering challenge: building “software factories” within teams and companies. Satya believes every company needs to control their AI infra – the harness, context, memory, model – and that verification of the generated code is a hard, currently unsolved, problem. Inside Microsoft, he sees lots of teams building their own “software factories” to improve team and org operations. As we talked, it became evident that building software factories looks set to be a widespread engineering problem across the industry because it’s a novel challenge without many existing “blueprints”. It will be slightly different for every team and company. There’s going to be lots of work in this space!

10. “Migrating” to AI is quite different from migrating to a new technology. We talk about how “migrating” to become “AI-native” feels similar to a brownfield project introducing a new technology, such as moving over from HTML+JavaScript to React. Satya also perceives some differences:

  • All tools are changing, not just a single technology: the runtime, the framework, and the concept of the IDE

  • When a new model launches with new capabilities, it can invalidate existing setups, just as models like Opus 4.5-and-above have invalidated IDEs.

11. Satya is very enthusiastic about decision models. Satya loves how decision models like ‘Jev’ and Microsoft’s ‘Decision-1’ are a kind of new primitive. He says: “These decision models are kind of like Excel macros. What happened to spreadsheets with macros can happen with code with intelligence embedded as a primitive. This primitive has a distribution, it doesn’t need to be generated again and again, it’s token-efficient. I think that this is one of those places where software engineering remains very much alive. Decision models are like the stored procedure of the intelligence era.”

12. Satya’s advice for winning with AI: stop reading & listening about it, and start using it more. He says:

“It’s ironic on a podcast to say, but it’s “do more, learn more, and be hands-on.” Experience it firsthand. If I could change the ratio of my “talk” to “do,” I would. This is the time. If there’s one piece of advice – whether you’re mid-career, a CEO, or a fresh college grad – it’s that the more you can take the time to learn, to be in teams that are doing it, then the better that is versus anything else I can think of.”

item.title: Software correctness & supply chain security, with Sean Allen
item.description: A deep conversation on the biggest challenges of developing with AI – while trying not to mention the phrase “AI” once. Why? To dig up the fundamentals that are as important as ever
item.dc:creator: Gergely Orosz
item.content:encoded:
Before we start, I’d like to share some exciting news: The Pragmatic Summit is returning! It’s a one-day event on 10 February in San Francisco, almost exactly one year after the first Summit. I’ll be hosting and the first few speakers are confirmed. Some faces may be familiar to regular readers and listeners!

My goal with the Summit is to make it the single best event for connecting with like-minded engineering leaders and engineers, and curious, driven people. Feedback from last year was that it was the attendees and the quality of debate that made it a standout event. We aim to deliver the same this time with the organizing team, including space for roundtable discussions, and talking with speakers who can stay around after their talk. The Pragmatic Engineer team shall be there too.

Applications are open: this summit is for senior+ engineers and engineering leaders who are shaping how modern engineering teams build software, ship products, and scale up to meet challenging demand curves. Tickets are priced at $1,000. You can check out last year’s talks, or watch a one-minute video summary.

This year’s Summit is made possible by friends at WorkOS, which is helping organize the event and is the exclusive sponsor. Thank you!

I hope to see many of you there! Now, onto today’s article.

Sean Allen is a software engineer with deep expertise in building large distributed systems, stream processing, and confidential computing. He is a core contributor to the programming language Pony, which is designed for concurrency. Sean is a distinguished engineer at Antithesis.

I was keen to talk with Sean due to his work on confidential computing at Microsoft, as well as his extensive work on the Pony language, and his passion for software correctness, which he works on fulltime at Antithesis.

For this conversation, we set ourselves the challenge of discussing modern software engineering without using the phrase “AI” a single time. Read on to see if it’s possible in 2026…

In this article, the questions are posed by me in bold font, with Sean’s words in normal font.

Today we cover:

  1. Software correctness & languages built for correctness. Why languages in the Meta Language (ML) family that are built around strong type systems catch more errors during compilation time than those in the Algorithmic Language (ALGOL) family.

  2. Does anybody care about testing? For someone passionate about correctness, Sean is surprisingly anti-testing. He argues that manual testing is the worst way to ensure correctness because you want illegal states to be prohibited from being expressed in a language – even before testing.

  3. Workloads & correctness. A more robust way of testing stuff than things like unit tests, is to define “workloads” that can be executed numerous times during a test. A common workload example is The Bank Test to stress test database isolation guarantees.

  4. Is quality a “gate” or not? It’s tempting to think of quality checks as closed gates that keep out poor quality. Sean pushes back against this; he says it’s important to consider quality from the very start, and to build with validation techniques that provide feedback on correctness. He prefers this to adding CI/CD quality “gates” late in the development process.

  5. Tech debt only hurts if you have to pay it back. Stop being afraid of tech debt because you often don’t need to pay it back at all! Sean says it’s common that tech debt is disregarded during rewrites when a system has become popular.

  6. No good fix for supply chain security. Supply chain attacks – when a package gets hijacked by an attacker and malicious code is executed on a machine or service – are very hard to defend against because languages with truly robust defenses, like ‘E’, are unpopular, while popular languages assume a trustworthy ecosystem. There’s no single or simple fix, says Sean.

  7. Garbage collection is slow – but doesn’t have to be. A summary of why garbage collection is devastating for runtime performance, and how Sean built a predictably performant approach in the Pony language.

  8. Go slow to go fast. Counter-intuitive advice: spend more time designing upfront and aligning everyone, and then you’ll move fast!

You can also watch this conversation on YouTube:

An amusing detail: Sean and I discovered we share in common a first fulltime employer. We both worked at a company called ‘Sense/Net’ at the start of our careers, although they were totally separate businesses in different countries. The founders of each must’ve been fans of the foundational cyberpunk novel, ‘Neuromancer’ by William Gibson, where the ‘Sense/Net’ name comes from.

Note: Antithesis is a podcast sponsor, but this deepdive is not sponsored by them. I’ve just been thinking a lot more about software correctness in the context of AI agents producing more code than ever, thereby creating opportunities for more bugs to ship to prod than ever. I wanted to learn more about this from an engineer with extensive experience in this area.

1. Software correctness & languages built for correctness

Gergely: How do you define ‘software correctness’?

Sean: “It’s down to whether my program does what I expect. I tend to talk about things in terms of ‘invariants,’ which is a more formal specification term. An invariant is a guarantee that my software does what’s expected of it. But here’s the problem: in lots of cases, people don’t know what they expect their software to do upfront! They know when it’s not working, but they don’t necessarily know what it means for it to be working.

‘Correct’ software does its business purpose and doesn’t wake anybody up at 2 a.m. with an outage. That is correct enough for me.”

Your personal definition of ‘beautiful code’ mirrors this.

Sean: “I was on the CoRecursive podcast when the subject of beautiful code in Ruby came up. I didn’t really know what people meant when they said ‘beautiful code’. Eventually, I came up with my own definition: beautiful code serves the purpose for which it was written and does not wake anyone up at 2 a.m.. That’s beautiful code to me!”

Early in your career, you programmed in the Ada language. What did that teach?

Sean: “When I was learning to program, I decided to pick a language and dedicate myself to it for a while. I ended up settling on Ada and C.

Ada was driven in a lot of ways by what the US defense department wanted: a language which is very deeply specified and will not let you write incorrect programs. NASA and the US Defense Department were the types who this language was aimed at. Ada still exists today, and the pitch that Ada companies make is ‘so, you like Rust, how would you like more correctness guarantees?’

One of my great regrets is I could not get programs to compile in Ada because I didn’t know much about programming back then. It was so frustrating!

Meanwhile, I could get C programs to compile, but they were segfaulting all the time! Over the years, I developed an intuition for how to do things in C so that my programs would not segfault and die. I had all these rules for writing concurrent C and C++ correctly. And even though I became really rigorous, I’m human and screwed up stuff.

C gave me almost nothing in terms of correctness. It was just a big gun that I pointed at my own foot and shot it off with, over and over again. Looking back, I understand the reason my Ada programs wouldn’t compile was that they were fundamentally memory-unsafe. And so, Ada refused to compile, given the program would have ended up with memory corruption, a crash, or a data race.”

What about languages in the ML family, like OCaml?

Sean: “When it comes to programming languages, there’s a few families:

  • ALGOL family: the foundation for imperative programming. These are block-structured languages with local variables. Languages like Python, Perl, Ruby, C, and C++ all belong here.

  • ML family: ML languages are built around strong type systems. Standard ML, OCaml, and F# belong in this family. Fun fact: Rust is the most famous ML-influenced language today. Rust’s sum types and pattern matching come from ML.

A sum type says ‘this value could be one of these things’, a bit like enumerations in Java. You combine that with pattern matching, and then with exhaustive matching. Say I have a sum type, which could be five different things. Instead of an if statement, I pattern match for which one it is. For example, here’s a sum type expressed in Rust:

Here’s the neat thing about a sum type: say you make a change to a sum type by going from five value types to six. As soon as you do it, the compiler will tell you every single place in your codebase where you’re not handling that sixth type, when combined with exhaustive matching! In other words, exhaustive matching turns every “forgot to handle the new case” bug into a compilation error. It is a gloriously wonderful experience to work with such a language.”

2. Does anybody care about testing?

You’ve written “no one cares about testing. I don’t value tests,” but it’s odd to hear this from you as someone who does care about correctness.

Sean: “I wrote that because people think of Antithesis as a testing company, and I don’t think of it that way. I think of it as a software verification and correctness company – which is very different.

Tests are things that you do to verify that things are working, for things you have no better way to verify. The worst type of testing is manual testing. You can automate it, and get more and more sophisticated with automated tests, but you are still doing something at the late stage of development. You should do as much as possible before you get to testing.

With ML languages, you can usually represent within the type system what the states are, and what the allowable transitions are. Once you have these in place, you can make sure that things can never transition to a state you don’t expect. Being able to do so is huge!

In practice, when you’re trying to work out whether your system works, you’re not thinking about the entire thing all the way down. You’re only thinking about the stuff your type system will not allow you to express. This is the idea behind “make illegal states unrepresentable.”

Playing devil’s advocate, you write the tests first in test-driven development (TDD), so that’s doing testing upfront, isn’t it?

Sean: “I love TDD. I think it’s one of the best mechanisms for writing great APIs because you’re actively looking at how you’ll work with the thing.

Also, the TDD community loves katas (little programming exercises). One of these is done in pairs: one person writes the test, and another writes the implementation which makes the test pass. The person writing the implementation is supposed to do the simplest possible thing.

When people did these katas with me, they quickly discovered that I took writing the least amount possible to pass very literally. I would hard-code answers into the implementation to make their example-based tests pass. For example, if the only test is ‘what’s 2 + 2?’, I would just return a hardcoded ‘four’.

You get to property-based testing with TDD katas pretty quickly. The kata isn’t supposed to end until the person writing the tests is happy with the implementation, so the only way to ‘beat’ somebody who’s as literal as I was, is to start randomizing the inputs. The moment you randomize inputs, you’re in the land of property-based testing because you’re generating inputs to cover more space than you’d come up with in examples.”

To be brutally honest, if I was writing the tests, I might think you were being a bit of a jerk!

Sean: “Make that a bit more profane, and that is what people said to me on a regular basis!

At one place where all the engineers did this exercise, whoever was paired with me would come out saying they were the only one who didn’t finish. But they’d also say, ‘I think I’m going to be much better at writing tests now.’

An awful lot of what was being tested with our katas were things you wouldn’t have to test with a stronger compiler. For years, I loved dynamic languages; Smalltalk is still one of my favorite languages, and I wrote a lot of Ruby, Perl, and Python. And I told myself I didn’t need the compiler’s help.

Eventually, I realized I could get by without much compiler help because I mostly worked on small systems, and I could hold everything in my head. When I started working on bigger systems at bigger companies with more people, I started to value things like being able to delete a class and have the compiler tell me every single place that breaks.”

3. Workloads and correctness

You’ve previously said that many people don’t have ‘workloads’ in their testing strategy. What are workloads?

Sean: “Most people’s examples of property-based testing are simple:

  • Reverse a list

  • → then reverse it again

  • → confirm you have the same list you started with.

However, if you want to apply property-based testing to a distributed system or database, then the workload is a combination of:

  • Inputs: created by you to drive your code

  • Validation: whatever you use to validate that the thing is working

For example, let’s take a key-value store with three operations. The workload is the combination of:

  • Inputs: the GET, PUT, and DELETE operations

  • Validation: deciding how many keys there are, what the range of keys is, and how big the key and their values can be

When reading about property-based testing, it’s easy to think that randomness is going to do the testing for you. For example, say you pick one of GET, PUT, and DELETE operations at random. By doing so, you won’t trigger many interesting places in your code because after a PUT, you’ll probably do a DELETE nearby. The odds of doing 10,000 PUTs in a row – pushing into areas where your store needs to swap to disk, garbage collect, or reshard – are tiny. Leaving all of this to chance is like walking when drunk: people don’t get very far from where they start.”

What’s a specific workload that can help with testing?

Sean: “There’s one workload commonly used for testing isolation guarantees in ACID databases, and it’s the single most important thing you want to guarantee in a database. It’s called the ‘Bank Test’:

Let’s take this setup:

  • There’s $10,000 in the system

  • You split this $10,000 between 10 accounts. Each account has $1,000.

  • The workload transfers money from one account to another inside a transaction

While running the workload which does transfers between accounts, you have another component constantly querying the total amount of money in the system. If the isolation guarantees hold, the only value it should ever see is 10,000.

If your database is good, you should never see weird failures. But if we’re talking about a distributed database and you run it in an environment where you introduce faults – like network ones between nodes or killing nodes – then all sorts of interesting bugs start popping out. Kyle Kingsbury made this famous with his Jepsen work on distributed systems safety research; it’s in the same vein as what we do at Antithesis.

A simple workload exercises a core invariant: in this case, the invariant is ‘I should never see the effects of an operation that is happening inside of another transaction.’

So, with a workload, you set the rules and let things work themselves out? And with this Bank Test, we never specify how much money to transfer or when: it just describes how transfers happen?

Sean: “Exactly. For software that’s been around for a while and has gone through rigorous testing, no bugs should pop out of something like the bank test. But bugs start popping out like crazy once you subject it to a Jepsen or Antithesis-type experience. That’s also the type of experience that happens all the time in production environments, which software engineer Lorin Hochstein does an incredible job of writing up in his incident breakdowns.”

4. Is quality not a “gate” or not?

You believe quality is not a gate. The “gate” concept rests on a belief that quality is something you hold by keeping out the bad – but this isn’t how good teams stay good. What do you mean?

Sean: “This is a big reason why I prefer talking about correctness rather than testing.

item.title: Scaling Slack and GitHub with Maude Lemaire
item.description: Maude Lemaire shares lessons from scaling Slack and GitHub, improving performance at Cursor, and using AI while keeping engineering judgment in human hands.
item.dc:creator: Gergely Orosz
item.content:encoded:
Listen and watch now on YouTube, Apple, and Spotify. See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom.

Brought to You by

• turbopuffer – The tpuf eng team is completely redesigning their storage architecture from first principles. And they’re documenting all of it! They made epic progress; take a look: turbopuffer.com/v3

• Antithesis – use AI agents to work on critical systems without worrying about correctness. Antithesis runs your complete system in a hostile environment, analyzes its behavior, and reproduces every issue perfectly. Learn more

• Entire – Entire launched its own Git forge, shipped Continuous Memory, and reinvented the pull request (called Trails). Trails are a much more natural workflow when agents keep pushing new changes, after iterating on feedback – and you have more context and control on when a change is ready to merge. Check it out

In this episode

What is involved in scaling up large, popular products at places like Slack and GitHub?

We get an insider’s view on this from Maude Lemaire, a principal engineer and author of ‘Refactoring at Scale: Regaining Control of Your Codebase.’ She spent nearly eight years at Slack, where she led the backend performance infrastructure team, before joining GitHub to tackle database scaling challenges. Most recently, she worked on improving performance at Cursor – including time to first token.

In this episode of The Pragmatic Engineer, Maude and I dig into the challenges of scaling some of the world’s largest software products. We explore how Slack handled growing numbers of enterprise customers, how it evolved its approach to load testing, and the lessons Maude learned during nearly eight years of scaling Slack’s infrastructure.

She also tells us what it was like joining GitHub in 2024 when Copilot was taking off, the challenges of working with GitHub’s gigantic Rails monolith, and how Maude uses AI in her work – while keeping judgment calls and decision-making firmly in her own hands.

Takeaways from the conversation with Maude

Here are eight interesting points from our discussion:

1. Performance should matter even if there’s no competition. In 2015, the homepage of Rent the Runway took up to 10 seconds to fully load due to a high-resolution hero image on the site. Maude was told it wasn’t an issue because there were no competitors to worry about. She thought differently: “The best competition is competition with yourself, knowing that you can do better, knowing that you can drive a better experience, ” she said. Maude spent some free time on speeding up the website without asking for permission to do so because it was the right call.

2. Slack limits custom emojis to 23 to avoid thundering herds. Here’s an example of a thundering herd: the CEO of a 100,000-member Slack channel posts “everyone gets Friday off!” In response, people start posting custom emojis – hundreds of them. The problem is that every single custom emoji has to fan out to all 100,000 users. With 10 custom emojis, that’s 1,000,000 fan-outs, with 100 it’s 10,000,000; a lot of network load! Slack limits custom emojis to 23 to avoid this problem. In reality, the absent 24th custom emoji is not missed.

3. Event floods can cripple the machines of Slack’s power users. Event floods are the cousin of thundering herds: they occur when a single client is overwhelmed by events coming through its own WebSocket. For example, when an IT worker is logged into lots of busy channels and they all receive the “everyone gets Friday off!” message – along with all the associated custom emojis and messages. This “power user” gets a sudden influx of messages with no deduplication and they struggle.

4. Load testing 500,000 WebSocket connections the simple way would have cost $150,000 per run. A new customer with 500,000 users was about to sign up to Slack, and Maude needed to run a load test to confirm the service could handle the load. Initially, she planned to spin up headless Chrome instances – each instance running a Slack session, and that would have cost $0.37 per five-hour session, per instance. The total price would’ve been crazily expensive. Instead, Maude built a tool called Koi Pond that spins up slimmed-down versions of Slack (‘Koi’), written in Go to establish the WebSocket connections.

5. Active Record downside: too much database load! GitHub used to be a Ruby on Rails monolith, which used Active Record as a database abstraction layer. This caused unexpected load: GitHub’s home page fetched live data from the database for most reloads, and loading the home page regularly triggered 100 SQL queries across three database clusters. This revealed a downside of abstractions like Active Record to Maude: when devs used it, they didn’t know or care about the additional load they unwittingly placed on the database while fetching data for whatever they were working on.

6. GitHub could not add more than 16 database shards because of scatter query problems. A scatter query is one without a primary key (a sharding key), and it needs to be run across all shard instances. But more shards make such queries slower.

Back in the day at GitHub, lots of queries made through Active Record (many on the homepage) were scatter queries. This limitation prevented GitHub from adding more than 16 shards. I find this detail fascinating: it shows why a developer-friendly abstraction (Active Record) can actually cause severe pain at the infra level!

7. For platform work, Maude personally verifies everything she gets from an LLM. When doing foundational work, Maude pays close attention to verifying the output of LLMs because she believes that ambitious structures can only be built on stable foundations. It’s an interesting approach to separate “foundational” and “non-foundational” work in order to give more attention to the former, most critical, type.

8. Platform and product engineers should rotate more. The best platform engineers Maude has worked with are product engineers who reimplemented similar features a few times, grew frustrated with the repetitive toil, and so built tools to remove it once and for all. But an issue arises when platform engineers become detached from product development and drift away from engineers’ experience of using the product. To remedy this, Maude suggests rotation cycles where a platform engineer joins a product team to build a feature, and a product engineer joins the platform team.
